questions.q: According to this lesson, what should you show first when presenting your capstone in an interview or portfolio review?
options: The Graph view, proving the real dependency structure in about thirty seconds
A slide deck describing the DAG without showing it running
The raw Python file with no explanation at all
A screenshot of an unrelated example DAG
questions.explain: The Graph view visually proves the real dependency structure exists, before anything else is discussed.

questions.q: When discussing the retry and alerting configuration, what does this lesson say you should be able to describe?
options: The deliberate failure you triggered to prove the alert actually fires, not just that it's configured
Only the exact syntax of the retries parameter, with no context
Nothing — retries and alerting aren't worth mentioning in an interview
A failure that has never actually been tested
questions.explain: Consistent with this course's habit of proving things work, the lesson recommends describing the deliberate failure that proved the alert fires for real.

questions.q: How should you answer 'What happens when the Snowflake load fails at 3 AM?' according to this lesson?
options: Retries happen first, then the alert fires, then someone investigates in the morning using a diagnostic checklist — not scrambling in real time
Nothing happens; failures are simply ignored
The entire Airflow deployment automatically shuts down
A human must be manually watching the screen at 3 AM for it to work
questions.explain: The lesson ties this answer directly to retries, alerting, and Lesson 28's diagnostic checklist — the whole point of building those safeguards.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what was this course fundamentally about, beyond DAG syntax?
options: Making eventual pipeline failures visible and recoverable instead of silent
Memorizing every Airflow operator by name
Avoiding the use of Python entirely
Guaranteeing that pipelines never fail
questions.explain: The lesson frames the entire course around the anxiety of unattended pipelines failing silently, and building habits (dependencies, retries, alerting, diagnostics) to prevent that.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does completing this course mean for the Analytics Engineer path?
options: It completes the entire seven-course path: T-SQL Development, Power BI, Snowflake, dbt, Git/GitHub/CI-CD, Data Factory, and Airflow
It is only the first course in a longer path still to come
The Analytics Engineer path has no defined end point
This course is unrelated to any other course in the catalog
questions.explain: This is explicitly the seventh and final course in the Analytics Engineer path, completing the full sequence from SQL through orchestration.
